1.pericope_label: In the second year of Darius the king, in the sixth month, in the first day of the month, came the word of the Lord by Haggai the prophet unto Zerubbabel the son of Shealtiel, governor of Judah, and to Joshua the son of Josedech, the high priest, saying, Thus speaketh the Lord of hosts, saying, This people say, The time is not come, the time that the Lord’s house should be built.

schools.summary: Ellicott fixes the king as the first Darius and disposes of the later identification by the men still living who had seen the first temple, notes the new moon as a fitting occasion, and treats the sonship as adoptive after a levirate marriage; Keil and Delitzsch confine themselves to what the headings yield and reject the extra-biblical accounts of the prophet's life as unsupported, and on the excuse keep to the grammar, hearing contempt in the phrase this people.

Gill rejects the Median and the later Persian kings by counting the years the officers would have had to serve, and notes that the title of hosts is prefixed to show the words are not the prophet's own; Calvin reaches the same king by the succession of reigns, dismisses the rabbinic genealogy as fancy, and argues that the absence of any real chronological excuse proves the delay was indifference.

Clarke supplies the political history of the revoked and restored edicts, insists that none of their own governors was absolute, and supposes they had simply miscounted the seventy years; Wesley notes the adoptive sonship and reads the high priest as a type of the great deliverer.

Henry sets the moment in the history of prophecy, the older prophecy making bright efforts before it expires, and draws the moral that a good work is put by simply by being put off, and that it is worse to plead providence in patronage of a neglect than to neglect a duty outright.

positions.position: The son of Hystaspes, since a later date would require impossible spans of office and life.
The first Darius; the later identification is absurd, being refuted by men still living who had seen the first temple.
The third king of Persia, the rabbinic genealogy making him son of Ahasuerus being a bold fancy.

debates.question: Why did the people say the time had not come?

positions.position: They miscounted the seventy years, though sixty-nine had in fact been completed from the last siege.
The chronology gave them no excuse at all, which proves the delay was indifference dressed in pretexts.
The ground is unstated, but was probably a pretended dread of Persian hostility.
Read as not yet time to come, that is, to assemble and build; the phrase this people carries contempt.
Strictly the son of Pedaiah, the sonship named being adoptive after a levirate marriage.
Son of Shealtiel, of the house of David through Jeconiah.

outliers.claim: Dismisses the traditional biography of the prophet, that he came from Babylon while young and was buried in honour near the burial place of the priests, as having no evidence at all to support it.

themes: In the second year of Darius the king, in the sixth month, in the first day of the month, came the word of the Lord by Haggai the prophet unto Zerubbabel the son of Shealtiel, governor of Judah, and to Joshua the son of Josedech, the high priest, saying,
Thus speaketh the Lord of hosts, saying, This people say, The time is not come, the time that the Lord’s house should be built.

3.pericope_label: Then came the word of the Lord by Haggai the prophet, saying, Is it time for you, O ye, to dwell in your cieled houses, and this house lie waste? Now therefore thus saith the Lord of hosts; Consider your ways. Ye have sown much, and bring in little; ye eat, but ye have not enough; ye drink, but ye are not filled with drink; ye clothe you, but there is none warm; and he that earneth wages earneth wages to put it into a bag with holes.

schools.summary: Ellicott calls the question about the panelled houses a crushing retort and notes that the results of their conduct are set out first so that its nature may be inferred; Keil and Delitzsch supply the grammar of the interrogative and the apposition, gloss the summons as attending to designs, actions and consequences, and read the repeated formula as sharpening the antithesis.

Gill marks the passage as a second prophecy addressed to the people themselves and notes the reversal of the ordinary case in the thin crop; Calvin explains why the refractory must be urged more sharply than the teachable, insists the catalogue of losses is past and not future, and distinguishes withheld produce from produce robbed of its nourishing power.

Clarke supplies the fourteen-year interval that makes the reproach bite, observes that the verse is a string of five proverbs, and states the condition flatly that no labour will be blessed until the house is built; Wesley glosses each clause to the same end, that food does not nourish, drink does not revive and clothing gives no comfort.

debates.question: Are the frustrated labours past or still to come?

positions.position: Past: those who render the clauses as future wrest the sense, since the call to consider would be pointless against a merely future punishment.
Past and continuing: the curse with which God has punished and is still punishing the neglect.

debates.question: What exactly is the curse in the catalogue?

positions.position: Two distinct things: produce withheld by drought, and produce given but robbed of its nourishing power.
Simple scarcity: there was not much to eat, drink or put on, and the pierced bag is a metaphor for prevailing poverty and high prices.
A thin crop from much seed, the blessing withheld from the earth because of their sins.

outliers.claim: Justifies the sharpness of the appeal on the ground that experience is the teacher of fools, so that when instruction and warning have failed nothing remains but that the people be drawn by force while they are chastised.

themes: Then came the word of the Lord by Haggai the prophet, saying,
Is it time for you, O ye, to dwell in your cieled houses, and this house lie waste?
Now therefore thus saith the Lord of hosts; Consider your ways.

Ye have sown much, and bring in little; ye eat, but ye have not enough; ye drink, but ye are not filled with drink; ye clothe you, but there is none warm; and he that earneth wages earneth wages to put it into a bag with holes.

7.pericope_label: Thus saith the Lord of hosts; Consider your ways. Go up to the mountain, and bring wood, and build the house; and I will take pleasure in it, and I will be glorified, saith the Lord. Ye looked for much, and, lo, it came to little; and when ye brought it home, I did blow upon it. Why? saith the Lord of hosts. Because of mine house that is waste, and ye run every man unto his own house.

schools.summary: Ellicott denies that any single mountain is meant, taking the term for the high lands where suitable timber grows, and reads the blowing as done to disperse what little was gathered; Keil and Delitzsch reach the same sense by making the article generic and reject both proposed identifications, adding that fetching wood stands for providing materials generally.

Gill allows either the northern range or the temple hill and locates the disappointed expectation in harvest and trade alike; Calvin reads the two summonses as the two stages of repentance, explains why so much weight rests on a building, and observes that scarcity stings most those whose desire had led them to seek abundance.

Clarke names the northern range and recalls the cedars already procured and the hired craftsmen wasted by the suspension, and turns the disappointed expectation against their conduct rather than their crops; Wesley glosses the promise as the acceptance of their offerings and the hearing of their prayers.

debates.question: Which mountain are they sent to?

positions.position: Either the northern range, for cedar, or the temple hill where the timber was to be carried.
The northern range, from which cedars had already been procured in the second year of the return.
No one mountain: the high lands generally, as the place where building timber grows.

debates.question: Where does the failure of their expectation fall?

positions.position: On the harvest and on trade together, a promising crop coming to little and riches diminished instead of increased.
On their conduct: they made great pretensions and did a little, but so scantily and unwillingly that it had to be rejected.
On what was gathered: even the little brought into the garner was reduced by continued disfavour.

outliers.claim: Answers why so much should rest on a building: the temple was of no importance in itself, but by it the people were kept in hope and taught to worship spiritually under external symbols, so that neglect of the fabric proved that no zeal for religion remained.

themes: Thus saith the Lord of hosts; Consider your ways.
Go up to the mountain, and bring wood, and build the house; and I will take pleasure in it, and I will be glorified, saith the Lord.

Ye looked for much, and, lo, it came to little; and when ye brought it home, I did blow upon it. Why? saith the Lord of hosts. Because of mine house that is waste, and ye run every man unto his own house.

10.pericope_label: Therefore the heaven over you is stayed from dew, and the earth is stayed from her fruit. And I called for a drought upon the land, and upon the mountains, and upon the corn, and upon the new wine, and upon the oil, and upon that which the ground bringeth forth, and upon men, and upon cattle, and upon all the labour of the hands.

schools.summary: Ellicott renders the disputed phrase on your account and would translate the calling of the drought as the invoking of a desolation, citing the parallel where a prophet announces a called famine of seven years; Keil and Delitzsch build the same force into their rendering, the heaven withholding its dew on your account.

Gill offers three constructions of the phrase and hears an elegant play on words by which a wasted house is answered with a wasting drought; Calvin uses the passage to state that God regarded not the visible building but the end for which it was designed, and draws from it a rule for teachers about applying the general curses of the law to present circumstances.

Clarke says only what the next verse shows, that a drought had been sent threatening scarcity and famine; Wesley notices that the visitation reached men themselves, their very blood and constitutions changed and many diseases afflicting them.

debates.question: What does the phrase rendered over you mean?

positions.position: Either upon you alone and not the surrounding nations, or that God is against you, or, with the Syriac and Targum, for your sake.
On your account, referring the cause back to the neglect just named.

outliers.claim: Draws a rule for teachers from the passage: since men in war or famine or pestilence do not of themselves regard the general curses of the law, those curses must be applied to them as circumstances require, so that they see God proving by facts what he testified in his word.

themes: Therefore the heaven over you is stayed from dew, and the earth is stayed from her fruit.

And I called for a drought upon the land, and upon the mountains, and upon the corn, and upon the new wine, and upon the oil, and upon that which the ground bringeth forth, and upon men, and upon cattle, and upon all the labour of the hands.

12.pericope_label: Then Zerubbabel the son of Shealtiel, and Joshua the son of Josedech, the high priest, with all the remnant of the people, obeyed the voice of the Lord their God, and the words of Haggai the prophet, as the Lord their God had sent him, and the people did fear before the Lord. Then spake Haggai the Lord’s messenger in the Lord’s message unto the people, saying, I am with you, saith the Lord.

schools.summary: Ellicott leaves open whether the word describing the people means those restored from exile or merely the remainder, and would render the following phrase in the Lord's message or on the Lord's mission; Keil and Delitzsch rule out the reading that would make the remnant the rest of the nation besides the two leaders, insist the prophet's title means messenger and not angel, and describe the promise as raising a penitent disposition into determination and deed.

Gill supposes the two leaders were the first to own their neglect and so set the example, and traces the notion that the prophet was no man but an angel to a rendering of his title; Calvin makes the leaders' precedence a rule about how any message works, takes the remnant for the small portion who actually returned, and turns the roundabout description of the obedience into an argument that God is not silent while ministers speak but speaks by their mouth.

Clarke states the result in a sentence, that where God's authority is acknowledged his words are carefully obeyed, calls the prophet the angel of Jehovah and defends the usage from the angels of the seven churches, and exclaims at the encouragement of the promise; Wesley glosses the message as spoken in the words of his master to the whole assembly.

Henry presses the humility of the two leaders, a governor who did not plead his former merits against a present reproof and a high priest willing to be taught, and observes that scarcity sharpens hearing, since manna rained in plenty is loathed as light bread.

debates.question: Does the prophet's title mean messenger or angel?

positions.position: Messenger only: the rendering angel gave rise to the notion that he was not a man at all.
Messenger, not angel, as many in the time of the fathers misunderstood it.
The angel of Jehovah, on the analogy of the pastors called angels of their churches.

debates.question: What does the remnant of the people mean?

positions.position: Either those restored from exile or merely the remainder of the people; the word will bear both.
The small portion who returned, against the great number who never used the liberty allowed them.
Not the rest of the nation besides the governor and the high priest.

outliers.claim: Argues from the wording that the church is not ruled by outward preaching as though God had substituted men in his own place and divested himself of his office, and that the word of God is not to be distinguished from the prophet's words as though the prophet added anything of his own.

themes: Then Zerubbabel the son of Shealtiel, and Joshua the son of Josedech, the high priest, with all the remnant of the people, obeyed the voice of the Lord their God, and the words of Haggai the prophet, as the Lord their God had sent him, and the people did fear before the Lord.
Then spake Haggai the Lord’s messenger in the Lord’s message unto the people, saying, I am with you, saith the Lord.

14.pericope_label: And the Lord stirred up the spirit of Zerubbabel the son of Shealtiel, governor of Judah, and the spirit of Joshua the son of Josedech, the high priest, and the spirit of all the remnant of the people; and they came and did work in the house of the Lord of hosts, their God, In the four and twentieth day of the sixth month, in the second year of Darius the king.

schools.summary: Ellicott supposes the intervening weeks were spent collecting timber in the upland region as the earlier command directed; Keil and Delitzsch give the stirring of the spirit and the dating plainly, without comment.

Gill describes the stirring as a rousing from sleep and sloth in which God worked both the will and the deed and removed the fear of men, and decides which reckoning of the month is meant by refusing to let the fitness of a building season govern the question; Calvin explains the delay as the difficulty of persuading them all to act with one mind, admits a mixture of weakness in it, and quarrels with whoever began the following chapter at this verse.

Clarke turns the stirring into a principle, that the judgment must be enlightened and the soul also invigorated before any good work can be effectually done, and measures the three weeks as a triumph of faithful reproof; Wesley fastens on the divine title as the one best suited to captives compassed on all hands with enemies.

debates.question: What filled the twenty-three days between the message and the work?

positions.position: Cutting stone and sawing and hewing wood in preparation.
Collecting timber in the upland region as the command had directed.
Persuading the people, since it was no easy thing to bring them all to undertake the work with one mind.
The preaching taking hold, so that by the twenty-fourth day the whole people were heartily engaged.

debates.question: Which reckoning of the sixth month is meant?

positions.position: The month answering to part of August; the other reckoning was chosen only because it seemed a proper season for building, and the fitness of the season is not in view.

outliers.claim: Complains of the ignorance of whoever began the following chapter at this verse, since the verse specifies the distance between the day he began to exhort and the success he is reporting, and therefore belongs with what precedes.

themes: And the Lord stirred up the spirit of Zerubbabel the son of Shealtiel, governor of Judah, and the spirit of Joshua the son of Josedech, the high priest, and the spirit of all the remnant of the people; and they came and did work in the house of the Lord of hosts, their God,
In the four and twentieth day of the sixth month, in the second year of Darius the king.
